text:
Angel Ortega, a teacher in New York, is dreading explaining to his students why he may no longer be able to teach next semester. Because his work permit as a recipient of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) expired before his renewal application was processed, he is currently unable to work.

In Springfield, Ohio, Rose-Thamar Joseph now dreads driving. As an individual with Temporary Protected Status (TPS) from Haiti, the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent decision allowing the Trump administration to terminate her status means she will likely lose her driver’s license and work permit soon.

Ortega’s and Joseph’s stories are not isolated accidents. Across the country, TPS holders and DACA recipients are losing the ability to work, drive, and ultimately continue their lives in the United States. The administration’s attacks on people with temporary protections – from ending TPS designations, to DACA renewal delays and seemingly indiscriminate detentions and deportations – lay bare how vulnerable immigrants are without a clear, legal pathway to citizenship. This underscores the importance of a procedure currently underway in the U.S. House of Representatives that could provide a solution to protect TPS and DACA holders.

“Death by a Thousand Cuts”: The Supreme Court’s TPS Decision and the Attacks on DACA Recipients

Temporary Protected Status (TPS) allows individuals from certain countries with unsafe conditions to legally live and work in the U.S. On June 25, 2026, the Supreme Court decided that no court can review a Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to terminate a TPS designation. The Court’s decision comes after former DHS Secretary Noem announced the termination of TPS for Haiti and Syria last year. It is expected to have ripple effects on all TPS-eligible countries, which may potentially be stripped of protection by this administration.

DACA recipients have also been under attack. Since summer of 2025, cases of DACA recipients being caught up in this administration’s detention and deportation agenda surfaced in news reports. Starting in February of this year, DHS revealed in various letters to Congress that hundreds of DACA recipients have been detained and that at least 86 DACA recipients have been deported. We have also heard countless cases of DACA recipients experiencing renewal delays. All this while we wait to see what the courts will do next on DACA.

Neither DACA nor TPS provide recipients with a pathway to lawful permanent residence or citizenship. If TPS is terminated for a certain country, the people protected by that designation will revert to their previous immigration status. If the person is undocumented, they may become at risk of detention and deportation. Similarly, if DACA recipients experience even a short period without DACA due to renewal delays, they lose their ability to work in the U.S. and become at risk of detention and deportation. Ultimately, the Supreme Court TPS ruling and the attacks on DACA demonstrate the fragility of temporary protections without a pathway to citizenship.

The Dream and Promise Act

As TPS and DACA holders anxiously plan their lives around court decisions and USCIS processing times, advocates have drawn attention to the Dream and Promise Act. The bill, which was most recently reintroduced in the House by Rep. Sylvia Garcia, would put DACA recipients, immigrant youth, and TPS holders who meet certain requirements on a pathway to citizenship. A pathway to citizenship allows individuals the ability to fully participate in the country they call home, without the fear of detention and deportation.

A Vehicle for Change: The Discharge Petition

The Dream and Promise Act has not been put up for a vote by the full House of Representatives since its reintroduction last year. That is where a discharge petition comes in. When the House Speaker refuses to schedule a vote on a bill, House members can force a vote if 218 members sign on to a discharge petition.

A recent inspiring and successful discharge petition was Rep. Ayanna Pressley’s petition on a bill that would extend TPS for Haitians by three years. The success of that discharge petition has given advocates and immigrant communities hope for advancing important legislation that remains stagnant due to divisive party politics. With so much at stake for DACA recipients and TPS holders, further inaction on the Dream and Promise Act could lead to widespread job losses, detentions, and deportations. For people like Angel Ortega and Rose-Thamar Joseph, the waiting game is a dangerous one.

text:
Washington, DC — Today, after the murders and ICE-related deaths in Maine, Texas, and Florida last week, amidst the deadliest years for immigrant detention in ICE’s history, and after members of Congress voted to fund the government through December, including DHS, Congresswoman Delia C. Ramirez (IL-03), immigration advocates, and impacted individuals stood together to demand that members of Congress pass the H.R. 7190, The Melt ICE Act. The bill would end the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) authority and funding to detain and monitor immigrants, disrupt immigration enforcement, and redirect funding back to communities for services.

Despite more than 50 members of Congress calling for the abolition, dismantling, or melting of ICE, only 13 members of Congress have joined the bill.

"DHS REMAINS the biggest threat to our collective safety. PERIOD. Americans are demanding members of Congress pursue more than training, more than reform, and more than bare-minimum policies. They are demanding that no other family suffers the pain of deportation or death at the hands of DHS's immigration enforcement," said Congresswoman Ramirez. "Today, we are saying it is time to Melt ICE and END the ICE AGE. Every single Democrat who is saying that it's unacceptable that DHS is terrorizing our communities must act and become a cosponsor of my H.R. 7190, The Melt ICE Act, to end detention, disrupt immigration enforcement, and redirect funding back to communities for services."

“ICE is shooting people who are going to work, taking their children to school, and even visiting as tourists. The death toll of ICE victims keeps rising. The actions of ICE’s masked death squads reflect the shameless cruelty of Trump and Miller’s policies, paid for by our tax dollars. It’s time to stop the ICE age and pass the Melt ICE Act,” said Congressman Jesús “Chuy” García (IL-04), cosponsor of the Melt ICE Act. “We must dismantle DHS and its for-profit detention centers, prosecute agents for their crimes, end the criminalization of immigrants, rebuild the enforcement system from the ground up, establish independent immigration courts, create safe and lawful pathways for migration, and actually fund case processing.”

"The ICE-related deaths we've seen in recent weeks are heartbreaking and unacceptable. They reflect a pattern of abuse, misinformation, and a complete lack of accountability that has put lives at risk for far too long. Time and again, ICE has shown time and again that it cannot be reformed. We need real action by passing the Melt ICE Act, ending our reliance on detention, dismantling ICE, and building an immigration system rooted in dignity, justice, and respect for human rights,” said Congresswoman Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), cosponsor of the Melt ICE Act.

“ICE agents are murdering people in the streets, tearing families apart, abducting our neighbors, and locking them in cages. ICE must be abolished – full stop. The billions of dollars that funded ICE should be given to the communities who suffered under their reign of terror. The Melt ICE Act, which I cosponsor, redirects funds toward housing, healthcare, and community organizations serving our immigrant neighbors,” said Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), cosponsor of the Melt ICE Act.

Ramirez was joined by Detention Watch Network, Immigrant Defense Project, Immigrant Legal Resource Center, and Bend the Arc to launch End The ICE Age, a new campaign calling on Members of Congress to shut down ICE detention centers, stop detention expansion, cut funding for ICE, and get ICE out of communities.

Ramirez was also joined by Sonimar Maria, the sister of Jesus Manuel Arenas Silva, a Venezuelan immigrant who was detained on July 13 and died in ICE custody two days after.

“ICE kills people, separates families, and threatens community safety across the country - full stop. No one is safe when ICE is present – whether on the streets or in one of the agency’s more than 200 abuse-ridden detention facilities. text:
Immigrants without criminal records make up 74% of the average daily population in California detention centers and 79% nationwide, according to data released this week by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The data shed light on how immigration detention has ebbed and flowed so far in 2026.

More than 43,000 people were booked into detention centers nationwide in June, the highest recorded since President Trump returned to office, the data show. Detentions had slowed since ICE launched large-scale raids across the country, including in Los Angeles in June 2025.

But detentions ramped up in late spring as Trump fast-tracked asylum cases, sowing confusion in immigration courtrooms as judges were forced to process up to 100 people or more in a single day. Many respondents missed their hearings and were issued default orders of removal.

The number of detainees booked in June was over 2% higher than the previous record of 42,107 in December, when federal agents launched a major operation in the Twin Cities that left two U.S. citizens dead, causing widespread outrage and prompting the Department of Homeland Security to shift its focus to the courtrooms.

In the nine months between October and June, 356,389 people have been deported, compared with 319,980 deportations for the 12 prior months.

ICE released the detention data on Monday after a months-long delay. The agency is required by Congress to publish data every other week, but hadn’t since early April.

The agency “has just ignored the law,” said Susan Long, co-founder of TRAC, a data gathering and research organization.

An ICE spokesperson said the delay was due to the partial government shutdown earlier this year, which closed the Department of Homeland Security for 76 days, before reopening in early May.

“The best way to ensure DHS can keep the public updated is to keep the agency OPEN and FUNDED, which thanks to President Trump is now guaranteed for the next 3 years,” the spokesperson told The Times.

The three-month lapse in data is the longest delay seen in years, said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. Consistent reporting of detention data is crucial to closely track shifts in immigration enforcement, he said.

“Immigration — it affects most individuals,” Long said. “We live in a democracy. For people to be able to meaningfully participate, they need to know what’s going on.”

The agency has nearly 66,000 people detained nationwide as of July 11, a jump from the last reported number in April, but still lower than a record high of 70,766 in late January.

The data doesn’t include people detained in short-term facilities, including ICE field offices and courtrooms.

The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown steered away from large-scale raids in recent months and instead shifted its focus toward legal immigration. Tactics include restricting asylum applications, packing immigration courtrooms and detaining immigrants who show up for routine check-ins.

The new data reinforced previous findings that the overwhelming majority of people detained by ICE do not have a criminal conviction.

Since October, on average, 6,412 people have been in detention on a given day across the eight California detention centers, 4,732 with no criminal record, according to a Times analysis of the data.

Only about 38% of the average daily population in custody at Adelanto ICE Processing Center have a criminal record. At the California City Immigrant Processing Center in Kern County, that number is 25%, the analysis found.

“The data continues to show that this administration is not focused on the worst of the worst,” Reichlin-Melnick said. “There has never been a time prior to the last year or so ... when the single biggest group that’s being arrested by ICE and sent to detention is people with no criminal record.”

Monthly detention numbers nationwide dipped well under 35,000 from February to May, according to the data. The lull followed intense immigration raids in January and the tail end of 2025.

Trump’s top border policy advisor, Tom Homan, told Fox News on Monday that monthly detention numbers dipped because of the partial government shutdown earlier this year.

The June spike in detention indicates continued efforts by the Trump administration to bolster its widespread immigration enforcement, Reichlin-Melnick said. “The system will continue to expand, and we should expect to see that throughout the rest of the year, though of course we don’t know exactly how that’s going to work.”

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — One Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer has been referred for discipline over a use-of-force incident since the beginning of the Trump administration, said Democratic members of the House Homeland Security Committee after a briefing with ICE officials Wednesday about body cameras, vehicle stops and training.

The closed-door briefing for committee members comes in the wake of two shootings in which ICE officers shot and killed two immigrants that they were trying to arrest, raising concerns over the agency's tactics at a time that it is ratcheting up its arrests.

The shootings in Maine and Houston over the span of a week have led to fierce criticism that there's not enough oversight of the agency key to President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration agents since Trump launched the crackdown after retaking office, and in the Maine shooting, family members of the ICE officer who opened fire say he had a history of violent behavior and never should have been given a badge and gun.

Rep. Seth Magaziner, a Democrat from Rhode Island, said they were told during the briefing that there have been 56 complaints of excessive force against ICE officers; 32 were cleared, and one was referred for disciplinary action. Magaziner said they were told no discipline had yet been handed out. The rest of the incidents are still under investigation, he said.

"It just defies belief that an agency of 20,000-plus officers with all of the chaos that we've seen over the last year and a half through the surges and civilians being injured and killed, that no one would be found to have violated use of force with the exception of possibly one person," Magaziner said.

Homeland Security said in a statement Wednesday that ICE officers who violate the agency's policies are held accountable, their officers are trained in de-escalation tactics and take an annual refresher course on use of force policies. The agency also defended its officers, saying they are operating in an environment where they are constantly being attacked.

"When faced with dangerous circumstances, DHS law enforcement professionals have used their training to protect themselves, their fellow officers, and the public," the agency said.

The use-of -force numbers mark an increase since February, when then-acting director Todd Lyons said during Senate testimony that ICE had opened 37 investigations for excessive force; 18 of those were closed, 19 were still pending, and one was referred for "further action," Lyons said.

The ranking Democrat on the committee, Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, said the ICE officials could not discuss the shootings in Maine or Houston, as those are both open investigations. Thompson, who said he came away with more questions than answers from the briefing, said he wanted to know who investigates use of force incidents: "Sometimes they said the FBI, sometimes they said HSI. Sometimes they said another entity."

The officials said they were going to retrain officers who had gone through a shorter curriculum that was in place last fall, Thompson said. In June, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the agency would be increasing the amount of training for new officers starting this month.

Thompson said he pressed for answers about how many officers had been brought back for retraining and how they're being retrained but couldn't get any clarity.

Thompson said he and the committee chair, Rep. Andrew Garbarino, R-N.Y., will follow up with ICE with a list of questions.

Garbarino said he appreciated ICE briefing the members.

"Today was an important opportunity for Members to receive timely answers on the status of body camera deployment for law enforcement in the field, training and vetting standards and requirements, and current guidance on the use of vehicle stops as part of immigration enforcement," Garbarino said in a statement.

When it comes to vehicle stops, Magaziner said they were told that current guidance to ICE officers is to only do them when there's no other alternative, and they're supposed to use lights and sirens. But, Magaziner said, that guidance has only been passed along verbally to the staff as opposed to a written directive.

Both the shootings in Maine and Houston involved shootings of immigrants who were in moving vehicles, raising questions about ICE's training and policies surrounding how it tries to apprehend people when they're driving.

After the Maine killing, Trump administration officials told ICE officers to suspend most vehicle stops. But the next day, Trump announced on social media that he wanted ICE to keep doing them.

text:
SUFFOLK, Va. — For the first time since his release from immigration detention, Victor Alfredo Perez Martin is speaking out about his July 6 arrest, his time in custody, and what comes next in his immigration case.

Video of Perez Martin being detained by ICE near Sentara BelleHarbour Outpatient Campus on July 6 has been viewed thousands of times online. ICE called it a targeted enforcement operation. A federal judge ordered Perez Martin released July 16.

Man seen arrested in viral video by ICE in Suffolk released from immigration detention

Speaking through a translator, Perez Martin said he, his brother, and a coworker were driving to work when they were pulled over.

"When they put me on the floor they pushed my face into the ground and then another guy came and put his knee on top of me. Then I had difficult breathing and I felt that I was being suffocated and that's when I try to push myself up," Perez Martin said.

ICE says Perez Martin was processed in Norfolk. His attorney says he was held at the Farmville Detention Center for nine days.

Perez Martin said he was able to speak with his family while there. Although medical care was offered after his arrest, he said he declined at first because he was scared. When the pain worsened the next day, he said he was told he would go to the hospital in shackles.

"What sense does it make to go to the hospital when they are going to keep me in shackles. It's just going to keep the shackles tight. I decided don't take me there just give me the medication to relieve the pain," Perez Martin said.

Rather than accept voluntary departure, Perez Martin chose to fight his case. He said the cost and danger of returning to the U.S. played a major role in that decision.

Undocumented immigrant in Suffolk ICE arrest now aims to stay in US, lawyer says

"The situation to return back to that country is a little complicated. I came here five years ago and it cost me $14,000 and nowadays it's more difficult and dangerous to come back here," Perez Martin said.

He said a conversation with his father reinforced his decision to stay and fight.

"He told me, 'If you can, try to fight so you can get out, because the situation back here is very hard. Where are we going to get that kind of money again?'" Perez Martin said.

When asked what he wants people to take away from the video of his arrest, Perez Martin said he is asking for any form of help.

"I have to pay for a lawyer I have to pay for the bond and with the economy you have to have security, the rent, your documents, and food," Perez Martin said.

His next court date is July 27.

text:
Why It Matters

The House Judiciary Committee advanced the Permanent Trump Secure Border Act on July 21, marking a significant victory for the House Freedom Caucus and aligning with the Trump administration's immigration enforcement priorities. The bill passed committee markup without external witnesses, instead featuring a legislative working session where House members debated 13 amendments, nearly all offered by Democrats, before the measure moved forward for potential floor consideration.

The Trump administration has made border security a centerpiece of its governance agenda. According to the White House, President Trump "promised to secure the border, enforce the law, and put American families first — and the data proves he is keeping that promise." The committee's advancement of H.R. 9773 signals Republican readiness to codify Trump-era border policies into law, a priority the conservative Freedom Caucus has been pressing House leadership to address.

The Big Picture

The House Judiciary Committee has spent more than a decade cycling through border and immigration enforcement legislation, with markup sessions stretching from the 112th Congress through the current 119th Congress. The committee's engagement with comprehensive immigration reform bills dates even further back, to the 110th and 111th Congresses in 2007–2009.

This year's push reflects a coordinated Republican effort to enshrine specific Trump administration policies. The House Freedom Caucus called for legislation to complete the border wall, end catch-and-release practices, and impose stricter asylum standards. As of January, Customs and Border Protection had awarded contracts for construction of 587 miles of border barrier, including traditional smart wall, water barriers, and secondary walls.

H.R. 9773 would restrict nonprofit funding by barring federal funds to organizations providing transportation, lodging, or legal services to inadmissible aliens. According to Bloomberg Government, "House Republicans advanced conservative border security legislation out of committee Tuesday, providing hard-right Freedom Caucus members a minor win and priming the bill for a possible floor vote."

What They're Saying

The markup session operated differently than a traditional hearing featuring outside experts. Instead, committee members debated amendments among themselves, with Democrats offering most of the proposed changes and Republicans largely rejecting them.

House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-OH-4) dominated the discussion, making 11 statements during the markup. Ranking Member Jamie Raskin (D-MD-8) made 2 statements, while amendment sponsors Zoe Lofgren (D-CA-18), J. Luis Correa (D-CA-46), and Chip Roy (R-TX-21) offered their perspectives as the debate unfolded.

The Democratic amendments faced steep odds. The Correa Amendment failed 14-16. The Jayapal Amendment tied 13-13. The McBath Amendment also tied 11-11. The Raskin Amendment failed 14-14. Several Democratic proposals were ruled not germane before reaching a vote, including amendments from Raskin, Lofgren, and Correa.

House Judiciary Committee Democrats characterized H.R. 9773 as "extreme" and "cruel." The session reflected the partisan divide over immigration enforcement, with Republicans unified behind advancing the bill and Democrats attempting to modify or block provisions they opposed.

Political Stakes

For the administration, the committee advancement validates its focus on immigration enforcement and border security as governing priorities. The bill's passage through committee positions it for a potential House floor vote, where Republican control of both chambers makes passage likely.

For House Democrats, the repeated amendment failures underscore their minority status and limited leverage in the legislative process. The tied votes on the Jayapal and McBath amendments, where Democratic members achieved parity but failed to prevail, illustrate the narrow margins at which they operate.

For the House Freedom Caucus, this represents tangible progress on a signature demand. The group has been pressing leadership for legislative action to cement Trump-era policies, and the committee markup delivers a concrete step toward that goal.

The bill's restrictions on nonprofit funding could have broader implications for immigration advocacy organizations and humanitarian groups operating at the border. If enacted, H.R. 9773 would reshape how federal resources flow to organizations providing services to immigrants in legal limbo.

The Other Side

FAIR, the Federation for American Immigration Reform, frames H.R. 9773 as preventing "future immigration crises," reflecting the conservative advocacy community's view that codification is essential to prevent a future administration from reversing Trump-era policies. This perspective underscores Republican concerns about policy continuity.

Reporting from NOTUS contextualizes the bill as "another try" after years of failed attempts at similar legislation, suggesting that despite Republican control of Congress and the presidency, translating campaign promises into law remains challenging.

What's Next

The bill now moves toward potential floor consideration. Speaker Mike Johnson controls the House calendar and will determine whether and when H.R. 9773 receives a full chamber vote. Given Republican majorities and Freedom Caucus pressure, floor action appears likely in the coming weeks.

Senate action remains uncertain. While Republicans control the upper chamber, any bill would need to navigate Senate procedures and potential Democratic opposition before reaching President Trump's desk.

The Bottom Line

The House Judiciary Committee's advancement of H.R. 9773 reflects unified Republican determination to lock Trump immigration policies into law while the party controls both chambers.

title: The Mental Health Cost of Harsh Immigration Policy - USCRI
description:
That’s why the effects of these policies extend so far beyond any one person’s immigration case.
Uncertainty Is Its Own Kind of Harm Living without stable legal status means living with the constant possibility that everything could change overnight.
None of this is a personal failing; it’s a predictable response to living for extended periods without safety or certainty.
Supporting that isn’t just compassionate policy — it’s a legal commitment this country has made.
USCRI will keep advocating for humane immigration policy and standing with the families living through this.
text:
Since January 2025, a wave of new policies has reshaped daily life for refugees, asylum seekers, and immigrant families across the country: the suspension of refugee resettlement, the possible return of “Remain in Mexico,” the end of humanitarian parole for thousands, temporary protected status at risk, and more.

Each of these sounds like a policy headline, but in practice, these changes are a daily source of stress for millions of people, including U.S. citizens with undocumented family members. This isn’t abstract. It’s showing up in how people sleep, work, parent, and plan for tomorrow.

Who’s Actually Affected

It’s a broader group than most people realize. Someone without legal status might have crossed the border without authorization, overstayed a visa, or fallen out of status through no fault of their own. But the reach of restrictive policy goes well past that population. Mixed-status families — where a U.S. citizen child has an undocumented parent, or siblings have different statuses — live with the same fear even though some family members are, on paper, fully protected. It’s the same with lawful permanent residents whose communities are being targeted by enforcement, and asylum seekers who are following every rule of the process but are still waiting years for an answer.

That’s why the effects of these policies extend so far beyond any one person’s immigration case. A single enforcement action can touch a household, a school, a workplace, and a neighborhood all at once.

Uncertainty Is Its Own Kind of Harm

Living without stable legal status means living with the constant possibility that everything could change overnight. Families avoid the doctor’s office. They skip school events. They turn down job opportunities, not because they don’t need them, but because being visible starts to feel dangerous.

That fear doesn’t stay contained to a single decision or a single day. It seeps into everything else: how well someone sleeps, how present a parent can be, how much a person can focus on work or school when part of their mind is always braced for bad news.

Living under that kind of pressure for months or years at a time takes a measurable toll. It’s associated with higher rates of depression and anxiety, and for many people who’ve already lived through violence or persecution, it can bring on symptoms of post-traumatic stress — nightmares, hypervigilance, flashbacks. Some people turn to alcohol or substances as a way of coping with the constant stress. None of this is a personal failing; it’s a predictable response to living for extended periods without safety or certainty.

Detention and Separation Leave Lasting Marks

Being held in immigration detention takes a real toll, even in facilities considered humane by any standard. For many, it echoes the very persecution or violence they fled in the first place. The loss of freedom, the isolation, the uncertainty about what happens next: these aren’t new experiences for someone who’s already survived trauma. They’re painfully familiar ones.

People held in detention show notably high rates of depression, anxiety, and PTSD, both while they’re detained and after they’re released. Some research on detained asylum seekers has found the majority experiencing significant symptoms of depression or anxiety, with roughly half showing signs of PTSD — figures that are hard to look at and impossible to dismiss as incidental.

Family separation compounds this. When enforcement actions split up parents and children, the effects don’t end the moment families are reunited. Kids who’ve been separated from a parent (even for a relatively short time) are far more likely to develop emotional and behavioral problems: trouble forming secure attachments, anxiety, appetite and sleep changes, withdrawal from peers, and behavioral outbursts. For some kids, these effects are still visible years after reunification.

The Limbo Itself Is Exhausting

Waiting indefinitely for an asylum decision, a status update, or news about a loved one’s case wears people down in a way that’s different from a single hard event. It’s ongoing. It touches nearly every part of daily life: healthcare, school, employment, safety.

Why This Matters Beyond the Individual

None of this is just a private hardship playing out behind closed doors. Communities lose neighbors, coworkers, and members. Kids lose stability at school. Local economies lose workers and taxpayers. The consequences ripple outward: to families, to classrooms, to clinics.

What We Believe

Everyone deserves due process, dignity, and a fair shot at safety, regardless of where they started. Supporting that isn’t just compassionate policy — it’s a legal commitment this country has made. USCRI will keep advocating for humane immigration policy and standing with the families living through this.

text:
Report argues that the Trump Administration’s bid to end asylum fails to provide long-term border solutions, harms U.S. economy

July 23, 2026 7:00 am

Media Contact

125 Broad Street

18th Floor

New York, NY 10004

United States

WASHINGTON— The American Civil Liberties Union today released a new report, Improving Asylum at and Beyond the U.S. Border, which explores how the Trump administration’s attacks on asylum and other humanitarian protections are weakening the U.S. immigration system already on the brink of collapse. The report argues that gutting asylum not only sends people with valid asylum claims to countries where they face death but also fails to provide long-term solutions for the border. The report comes weeks after the Trump administration deported at least two dozen people, including people fleeing persecution in Iran and Afghanistan, to the Central African Republic, one of the most dangerous places in the world. Its release also comes just days before the 75th anniversary of the United Nation's adoption of the 1951 Refugee Convention, a landmark treaty that outlines core legal protections and rights that States must uphold to protect refugees.

The report argues that attempts to gut our asylum system do nothing to prepare for future increases in arrivals along the U.S.-Mexico border. Adding obstacles to the asylum system means that political dissidents from Iran, LGBTQ persons from Uganda, children fleeing traffickers and many others can’t get the protection they deserve. At the same time, these restrictions don’t improve border processing, respond to new arrivals, or address the overdue need for lawful pathways, which has created demand at the border. Without needed reforms and legal options to come reunite with family, work, and seek safety, the government is sacrificing vulnerable people and its legal obligations while failing to create a sustainable alternative system that serves U.S. values, laws, and the economy.

“The Trump administration’s cruel anti-asylum policies are predicated on the false notion that by gutting humanitarian protections, our broken immigration system will somehow be fixed – but deporting vulnerable people to war zones, detaining families, pushing kids through mass hearings, and arresting refugees who followed the rules do not create a functional system,” said Sarah Mehta, report author and deputy director for policy and government affairs, immigration at the ACLU. “If our policymakers want any semblance of a fair and workable immigration system, they must commit to rebuilding asylum and creating other legal pathways.”

Though many of the arguments to close the border and the country to newcomers have focused on zero-sum thinking and promulgated claims about how people seeking asylum have strained local communities, the report highlights how asylum seekers and refugees are critical to a thriving U.S. economy and need support in getting to communities eager to receive them. For example, in 2024, asylees and refugees contributed an estimated $581 billion in revenue to federal, state, and local governments over a 15-year period, strengthening the case for improved access to asylum as communities nationwide, especially in rural areas, continue to feel economic strain.

The report urges policymakers to recommit to protect asylum and other existing humanitarian protections and invest in modern solutions to our border. Recommendations include:

Create additional lawful pathways for people to come to the U.S. to ensure that people can lawfully apply for and receive permission to come to the United States, without burdening the border arrival system.

Invest in border processing and modernize the arrival triage system so that people arriving at the U.S.-Mexico border with valid asylum claims can be processed quickly.

Support states and localities in welcoming newcomers through legislative solutions to improve coordination between arriving immigrants and the communities receiving them so that humanitarian needs and services are met and that communities have the support they need.

Fund and bolster the immigration court and asylum processing system to address backlogs, streamline bureaucratic processes, and enhance due process through legal representation.

It is the second report published as part of the ACLU’s affirmative vision series in which policy and legal experts will explore how the Trump administration’s immigration agenda has harmed communities nationwide, gutted asylum and other legal pathways, undermined our democracy, and wreaked havoc on key industries and weakened the American workforce. The series will also outline steps that members of Congress, as well as state and local policymakers, can take to reform the U.S. immigration system and inoculate against future attacks on immigrant communities.

You can read the full report here: https://www.aclu.org/publications/improving-asylum-at-and-beyond-the-u-s-border-the-case-for-a-fair-and-effective-protection-framework-with-a-modern-border-and-reception-system

Fresh from a trip to Haiti, US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz offered the UN Security Council on July 20 a harrowing account of the “kill zone” he said Port-au-Prince has become. In unusually graphic detail, he recounted grotesque incidents, including one in which several Haitian national police officers “were flayed alive in the streets [and] pinned to the side of their burning armored vehicle.”

Consistent with Waltz’s report, a July 10 State Department travel advisory warns: “Do Not Travel to Haiti,” citing “robbery, carjackings, sexual assault, and kidnappings,” and even the “risk of being struck by stray bullets,” saying that violence “happens frequently.”

And yet, the same government that describes horrors before the UN Security Council and certifies the country as too dangerous to travel to is preparing to deport some 350,000 Haitians there, as the US Supreme Court stands aside and allows the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

Mass deportations would put these people in grave danger and exacerbate Haiti’s humanitarian crisis. Many would be compelled to rejoin families living in dangerous areas where, perceived as wealthy, they could become targets for kidnapping and extortion.

It’s not too late. A new Homeland Security secretary is in place, Markwayne Mullin, who could still recognize Haiti as unsafe and extend TPS. It will take some convincing: after the Supreme Court ruling, he called upon Haitians to self-deport, offering them $2,100 to go back. But maybe the fact that the Federal Aviation Administration prohibits US air carrier flights to Port-au-Prince due to ongoing instability will give him pause.

The Supreme Court’s ruling is due to go into effect later this month. Secretary Mullin should listen to the words of the US ambassador to the UN and heed the State Department’s warning that, in fact, applies as much to Haitians as to US citizens: Do Not Travel to Haiti.

text:
David Brouillette, the ICE officer who allegedly killed Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during a traffic stop in Maine last week, had a history of domestic violence and a number of serious mental health issues, his ex-wife told NPR.

The killing, along with a fatal ICE shooting in Texas the week before, comes on the heels of a rapid hiring spree at the federal agency: ICE says it has hired more than 12,000 officers in less than a year. That has prompted some law enforcement experts to worry that ICE is cutting corners in its hiring – a lesson police have learned the hard way over the years.

"This is a person that never should have been hired," Gil Kerlikowske, a former commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, says of Brouillette. A typical vetting process should have caught red flags in the ICE officer's past, Kerlikowske told NPR.

When it comes to assessing an officer's mental well-being, hiring practices at police agencies around the country vary widely. But Kenneth Corey, who spent more than three decades at the New York City Police Department, says more intensive vetting, such as mandatory psychological evaluations, is becoming more common.

Corey oversaw the NYPD's medical division, including the psychologists who evaluated recruits. He says candidates there go through medical and psychological exams, and what is known as a background character investigation.

"If the investigation is done properly, you're contacting former employers, you are getting records and not just academic records, but specifically disciplinary records from schools," says Corey, who now leads the Policing Leadership Academy at the University of Chicago Crime Lab.

"You're contacting the police departments in any jurisdiction where your candidate has ever lived. Do they have any reports on file with your name on it? That would include domestic incident reports. It would also include cases where you were moved to a hospital for mental health issues," he says.

The process isn't perfect. Corey says at some agencies, for instance, if an officer is hired from a different police department, the new agency might assume the previous department did its due diligence. That can open the door for troubled cops to hop from one police department to another.

The job itself can also exacerbate existing issues, and stigma may keep some officers from seeking help. The stress that police officers experience is associated with higher rates of divorce, alcohol abuse, heart disease, post-traumatic stress disorder and depression.

"You want to make sure that the people you're hiring have the temperament and disposition necessary to do the job. It's a difficult job. It's oftentimes extremely stressful," Corey says. "You want to make sure you're hiring good quality people."

Corey stressed that proper officer training is also key. All of that – making good hires and then setting them up for success – takes time.

In the case of the recent ICE shooting in Maine, it's unclear whether the agency did not conduct proper vetting or overlooked warning signs. In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security says it applies all the "proper personnel vetting regulations" but did not provide specifics.

But the agency has hired a huge number of officers in a short time. Kerlikowske says when he ran Border Patrol, he had to resist pressure from Capitol Hill to move faster.

"The complaints would always be like, 'Well, you still have a thousand agents you need to hire.' You could explain, though, to members of Congress, to the appropriators, that, 'Look, we don't want to rush the hiring process,'" Kerlikowske says. "The mistakes that are made are significant. And you pay a huge price later on."

There are infamous examples of police departments hiring too fast with disastrous results.

"What police departments have learned over the years is that one officer hired without a proper background investigation, including a thorough psychological examination, can severely damage a police department's credibility with its community," Chuck Wexler, executive director of the Police Executive Research Forum, told NPR.

In 1989 and 1990, for instance, the Metropolitan Police Department in Washington, D.C., rushed to hire hundreds of police officers, cutting corners on background checks, psychological testing and training. Members of that hiring class were disciplined, arrested, charged with crimes, and fired in record numbers.

In the 1980s, Miami doubled the size of its police force in less than two years in an effort to combat violent crime. Dozens of police officers, many of them recent recruits, were eventually disciplined for actions related to police corruption, and many were convicted of crimes related to stealing drugs from traffickers.

In the years after the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, CBP, part of the newly created Department of Homeland Security, saw a massive hiring surge. Later, a former commissioner at the agency admitted that during its streamlining or elimination of vetting procedures, the agency had hired drug cartel members into its ranks.

"When you have pressure to hire a certain number of individuals during a certain time limit, then that's where, sometimes, steps may be overlooked," says Tanya Meisenholder, director of police research at New York University School of Law's Policing Project.

Meisenholder, who spent nearly 20 years at the NYPD and oversaw its hiring, says after the latest ICE shootings, the agency should take a serious look at any changes it made to hiring practices in the last year – and at any officers who were hired in that time.

title: The Trump Administration is Pushing a Culture of Hate | Opinion - Newsweek
description:
There is no doubt about it: the Trump administration is pushing a culture of hate, and our elected leaders aren’t responding.
To Americans everywhere: now is the time to demand more of your public officials.
Already gerrymandering attempts have spread across the country to limit fair representation for Black communities.
We will not allow our elected officials to sit idly by while people are hurting.
To my fellow elected officials, I ask that you join me in doing more than simply making statements on the critical issues affecting people's lives.
text:
Anytime I turn on the news, I worry about what I will see. Everywhere we turn there are people lying, screaming and spewing the same vile talking points. Some of the most powerful people in our country are doing everything they can to take away the rights, liberties and representation of Black people, immigrants, the LGBTQ+ community and all marginalized communities. They are dividing communities and fostering distrust, discrimination and violence.

There is no doubt about it: the Trump administration is pushing a culture of hate, and our elected leaders aren’t responding. In a system explicitly designed for checks and balances, we’re not seeing a whole lot of either. To Americans everywhere: now is the time to demand more of your public officials.

Our country was founded on the admirable idea that, when faced with an unjust government, it is the people's right and duty to reject that government and build a better one. Our systems were designed so that no one man could wield all the power and abuse it.

Read More on Opinion

These original ideals are being tested now, and we must rise to the occasion. When the people are faced with hate and vitriol, true leaders meet it with the full force of justice, equity and progress.

Yet, too many of our current members of Congress are praising the president and excusing government overreach to protect themselves. Other leaders are saying they won’t accept any more injustice, then sitting back down so no one calls them disruptive. Or, they are saying nothing at all so as not to make waves.

Our country deserves public servants who actually serve the public instead of themselves.

When the government is denying Black people, immigrants and marginalized communities of their due process, their life and liberty, it is not enough for the people in charge to write strongly worded letters or give speeches about how it’s wrong. It is our responsibility to take action and put ourselves on the line to get in between our constituents and the arms of cruelty and fascism.

Black, Brown, immigrant and working-class communities know all too well that words without action from politicians will get us nowhere. We have been on the front lines of the hateful policies and actions of this administration.

In Florida alone, more than 400,000 people hold Temporary Protected Status. Now, all of them have been left in the lurch because of Trump and his lackeys. Parents, neighbors and co-workers who were documented are now facing the terrible question of how to care for themselves and their families.

Our communities face an added danger just by existing; in the span of a week, two men were fatally shot by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers (ICE) and a third died while fleeing an encounter with immigration agents. Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father of three, was shot on his way to work. Joan Sebastian Durán Guerrero, a young father, was shot and pulled out of his car. Not far from my district, ICE was following Juan Jairo Coronilla Duran, a tourist, when he was struck by a truck and died.

All the while, the administration is trying to silence our voices. The gutting of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 this spring paved the way for those in power to protect their positions by drawing us out of our maps. Already gerrymandering attempts have spread across the country to limit fair representation for Black communities.

None of this should be normal. We will not allow our elected officials to sit idly by while people are hurting.

As a Florida State Representative, as a U.S. Senate Candidate, and above all as a mother, I am refusing to let this moment pass over me. I am putting my body on the line because that is what the position calls for. No matter the roadblocks, I will not stop because people are still hurting.

To Black, Brown, immigrant and all marginalized communities across the country, your voice matters. Now is the time to demand more from your lawmakers. Despite the challenges of the moment, we can put an end to the cycle of hate if we join in our demands for justice.

To my fellow elected officials, I ask that you join me in doing more than simply making statements on the critical issues affecting people's lives. The power of public servants is a privilege, and we cannot let it go to waste. You have the means to make change, so make it. Show up and present solutions that protect the people as you promised.

As Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. told us, the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends towards justice. This culture of hate will be defeated, so long as we never stop fighting.

title: Surprise health inspections remain legal, for now, at ICE detention center in Tacoma
description:
The state of Washington could still conduct unannounced health inspections at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma.
As things stand, the Washington State Department of Health is free to perform unannounced health inspections at the center.
Concerns about the sanitary conditions at the detention center have led to a series of hunger strikes by people detained there.
The woman, who KUOW is not naming to protect her from potential retribution, has been detained at the Tacoma center for several months.
The detained woman said she hopes for a future where detention centers like these are shut down.
text:
The state of Washington could still conduct unannounced health inspections at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma. That’s despite a recent lawsuit filed by GEO Group, which runs the facility, trying to stop surprise inspections by the state.

As things stand, the Washington State Department of Health is free to perform unannounced health inspections at the center. That’s been the case since May, when a new state law cleared the way for such inspections and provided money for staffing.

“The new law was effective on May 11, 2023, and the Legislature allocated funding to hire staff effective July 1, 2023,” said Kara Kostanich, spokesperson for the Department of Health.

Concerns about the sanitary conditions at the detention center have led to a series of hunger strikes by people detained there.

The surprise inspections would be welcomed by some detainees, including a woman who spoke to KUOW after taking part in a recent hunger strike. The woman, who KUOW is not naming to protect her from potential retribution, has been detained at the Tacoma center for several months.

“The showers never get scrubbed. They only get sprayed and wiped. They're moldy and the paint that's coming off the walls and it's all like it's all scratched in moldy and dirty,” she said.

The detained woman said she hopes for a future where detention centers like these are shut down. She spends her time learning, reading, and thinking about her children back home.

She had a green card but was part of a domestic assault case. After she found out her then partner was abusing her daughter, she said she decided to take matters into her own hands and attacked her partner.

Her daughter is now raising money for other sexual assault survivors.

After she spoke with KUOW, the woman said she was threatened with being put into solitary confinement by ICE detectives.

Another man being held at the Tacoma facility was handed over to ICE custody for deportation after spending several years in California prisons. He said conditions are worse in Tacoma than back in his California prison days.

“I used to be in the criminal system but I’m not in the criminal system. I'm just being detained, you know, I shouldn't be treated like a criminal when I’m being detained,” he said.

Legally, detention centers are classified as civil detention facilities, and not meant to hold people in the same way jails or prisons do.

Up until 2021 detainees were paid a dollar a day or given extra food to clean or cook until the GEO group lost a minimum wage lawsuit.

KUOW has reached out to GEO Group for comment about the inspections and their lawsuit, but company representatives did not immediately respond.

title: Migrant Rescue Operations Navigate a Mediterranean Bloodbath - Jacobin
description:
Seabird is operated by German NGO Sea-Watch to monitor violence on the world’s deadliest migration route alongside its rescue vessels.
On the coast, a migrant boat trapped on a cliff has become a monument due to the impossibility of removing it.
Despite mutual mistrust, activists and law enforcement personnel are both present and agreeing on the urgency of rescue.
For a decade, this force has been developed and funded by the European Union and Italy to prevent migration.
We open a window to photograph a rescue vessel below and air rushes in from a bright sea and sky.
text:
Seabird is operated by German NGO Sea-Watch to monitor violence on the world’s deadliest migration route alongside its rescue vessels.

It flies from Lampedusa’s tiny airport, a fifteen-minute walk from the town center. This diminutive island, an Italian possession on the African plate, laces worlds together. There is a rural community of a few thousand in barren backcountry. There is the resort swarming with pleasure crafts and tourists, leaving barely a free inch on TripAdvisor’s “world’s best beach” award–winning Rabbit Beach. There are the refugees landing and humanitarians assisting them. And there’s the former Cold War US spy stations and air force bases, girded with new border infrastructure.

Lampedusa rises and falls with empires. After the Romans left, traces of its habitation declined until the emergence of European imperialism. Today, its energy grid depends on imported diesel, which also powers the desalination plant producing salty tap water. Drinking water comes by ferry. Fresh water trickles in a cave in the Sanctuary of the Madonna, where legends say a hermit once sheltered both Christian and Muslim refugees. Lampedusa is unique but reflects the outside world shaping it.

Even in early summer, harsh gusts whip the coast. Stiff winds bend the remaining trees, but the hardy flora mostly hug the ground. Crosswinds rattle my flight to the island as it drops sharply inward. Lampedusa is thought to have been deforested by prisoners shipped from mainland Italy before the Risorgimento. Today a carceral migration economy still frames it.

Before we land, we glimpse the Porta d’Europa, a memorial sculpture to those dead at Europe’s gateway. It is ethereal; appearing less a doorway between continents and more one to whatever lurks beyond this life. The wider island is a mausoleum for border tragedies.

Above the port, the Garden of the Just honors rescuers; in a mural above it, a local woman embraces another life-jacket-clad woman. In the archaeological museum, Roman pottery fragments sit below paintings inspired by shipwrecks. On the coast, a migrant boat trapped on a cliff has become a monument due to the impossibility of removing it.

Beside the Porta d’Europa lies a rabbit warren of crumbling old military fortifications. The door is guarded.

A day before I arrive on Lampedusa, fifty people are rescued by Italy’s Guardia di Finanza (GdF), a militarized police unit. Italy’s coast guard and the GdF carry out most rescues, but unlike seagoing NGOs, they generally operate closer to home.

They bring ashore a one-month-old baby girl from the Ivory Coast, dead of hypothermia on arrival. Charity Mediterranean Hope organizes a vigil for her, departing the steps of a church whose crucifix was donated by the late Pope Francis following an infamous 2013 shipwreck. The new Pope, Leo XIV, has now also visited. The parade pauses at the town library, where a young Palestinian woman and her friend sing an Arabic lullaby in elegy, before dispersing on the harborside promenade at sunset.

Afterward we descend to a bar carved into cliffs, hosting a concert with a brew of Mediterranean influences, slow and haunting at first, rising to foot-stamping crescendos. The tragedy is on everyone’s minds, but the mood is convivial. Despite mutual mistrust, activists and law enforcement personnel are both present and agreeing on the urgency of rescue. One older GdF agent plays “Bella Ciao” on the guitar.

Outside sits the crew of Nadir, fresh from a rescue during which Libya’s Coast Guard (LCG) — in reality, a bundle of militias — harassed and threatened them. For a decade, this force has been developed and funded by the European Union and Italy to prevent migration. Libyan forces’ extreme violence and tendency to profit from smuggling have not stemmed European funding.

Within hours of the Nadir incident, rescue vessel Sea-Watch 5 was approached in international waters by a Libyan patrol boat that opened fire with automatic weapons without warning. Boats pursued the crew and ninety rescue survivors for hours. Italy subsequently ordered the ship on a needless four-day journey to safety. Instead of holding the attackers accountable, Italy opened a criminal investigation into the captain; the latest in a string of similar cases that have all collapsed in court.

Sea-Watch has now documented seventy-seven violent incidents involving the LCG. Things reached a head in August 2025, when rescue ship Ocean Viking was fired at for twenty minutes by a European-provided Libyan vessel. The international crew (from across four continents) petitioned their respective governments to little avail. When British crewmembers asked their government to respond, a minister replied with a curt “no.”

Despite attempted murder cases lodged in France and Italy over the Viking incident, Europe doubled down. New boats were transferred to Libya in December 2025. The unrecognized Eastern Libyan government was brought into the fold, with both rival governments present on a junket to Brussels.

As the Sea-Watch 5 was attacked, Council of Europe ministers adopted the Chișinău Declaration, a bid to dilute international refugee law led by Britain’s Keir Starmer and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen. Their position was that protecting citizens from perceived threats justified suspending rules. This hardly squares with the border machine’s outcome at sea: permitting a foreign military to attack European citizens in Europe’s backyard.

The European Commission insists its Libya financing is improving the situation. But there’s scant evidence of this, and plenty of proof that EU policy incentivizes violence. One Italian military official I spoke to privately agreed that cooperation with Libya was indefensible. But evidence of the harm being done, and even the strategy’s ineffectiveness on its own terms, goes ignored.

Shortly following the attack, humanitarians on the Gaza flotilla were abducted in international waters by Israeli forces. Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s revelry in violence against them produced condemnation from European leaders — which has not been forthcoming in multiple previous incidents.

Abuses beget abuses. The erosion of international law in Europe’s borderlands preceded EU institutions’ permissiveness toward genocide in Gaza, which in turn further normalized extreme violence globally. Criminalization and deportation of anti-genocide activists has stitched together authoritarian domestic and foreign policy. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids, drownings at European borders, and great-power aggression from the United States in Iran to Russia in Ukraine heralds a politics defined by unrestrained force.

As the Earth heats, the United States has embarked on a military takeover of fossil fuel networks to buttress its declining power; air strikes in Nigeria, kidnapping Venezuela’s president, threats to Greenland, and a firestorm against Iran. While capitalism’s fossil fuel dependence primarily threatens planetary health through climate change, the wars it provokes are now perhaps a more immediate threat.

In the Mediterranean and Africa, the US strategy merges migration control, military power, and resource access, cutting dozens of opaque deals to dispatch deportees to African states, a policy echoed in new EU deportation legislation. Libya has been both earmarked for exploitation by Chevron, and for a US deportation camp.

As the Hormuz crisis unfolded (in turn spiking fuel costs for both humanitarian and enforcement operations on Lampedusa), Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz was attacked crossing the central Mediterranean. The raid risked environmental catastrophe. The worst was prevented, but Ukrainian and Libyan forces’ growing entanglement raised questions, especially when another explosives-laden sea drone was found drifting in the Mediterranean in May. Russia is also competing for influence in both Libyan states.

Simultaneously, Italian ships began constructing new Libya gas infrastructure. As Gulf supplies become unreliable, Mediterranean deals will become more essential to Europe, adding new incentives to disregard human rights or environmental concerns. While Italy proclaims its North Africa strategy as transcending colonial history through cooperation, its model is anchored in fossil fuel extraction, arms, and violence — as Italy revives the pledge of a naval blockade against migration.

We view the consequences from Seabird’s windows as construction below begins, and an empty stretch of sea is suddenly crowded. Amid these waters marked by the deaths of people crossing, we can also glimpse an epochal scale of death; dying seagrasses, new marine parasites, fires and storms spreading.

Neeske Beckmann has been Seabird’s tactical coordinator for the best part of a decade. Alongside crimes against humanity, she has seen what else people hide in the sea; illegal gas flaring, a dead cow dumped from a livestock carrier, and arms shipments flouting the ban on weapons to Libya, which states from Turkey to Italy stand accused of violating. Rome has bet big on its military-industrial complex, with little apparent regard for human consequences.

“We’re seeing more guns on [Libyan] boats recently”, Beckmann adds. She recalls seeing a patrol boat they were observing carrying a rocket launcher. Seabird immediately climbed clear; LCG crews have threatened to shoot down monitoring aircraft.

Crews subsequently raised the minimum operational altitude for future flights. Such is the logic of operating in war zones, but this is a stretch of water that most Europeans associate with bucolic holidays. Profiteers from across the globe are cashing in, while the Mediterranean becomes more dangerous for all.

“I don’t want to express too much empathy for [Libyan forces], because their violence is horrendous”, says Beckmann. “But I’d like them to be able to see the bigger picture; that they’re being used too; that European powers benefit from their continued destabilization.”

Two days after we overfly the oil platforms, Seabird spots a Libyan boat driving south with seventeen people it has intercepted. It’s the Ras Jadir, an EU-provided vessel involved in the attack on Sea-Watch 5. Nearby, five people wait trapped on the abandoned Didon oil platform.

“It’s an assumption,” says Beckmann, “but we believe that Frontex coordinated the interception.” Their aircraft was on scene long before issuing a general distress call, she says, and Libyan patrols arrived suspiciously quickly. A 2022 Human Rights Watch report found that Frontex systematically referred people crossing to Libyan forces.

The central Mediterranean is, in fact, among the world’s most surveilled stretches of water, in the search for weapons, migrants, or drugs. This makes Europe’s collective failure to prevent record deaths more striking.

Surveillance forms many states’ vision of how a chaotic world can be made more secure and predictable, a vision that the ballooning AI-powered tech industry is keen to reinforce. All patterns, it says, can be spotted and managed. Crime can be prevented and even predicted. War can be mechanized through drones and AI targeting.

Frontex’s ambitious Mediterranean surveillance programs, comprising multinational data harvesting, drones, and satellites are an example; ostensibly about technocratic management, in practice tied to chaotically violent regimes. The violence is concealed by mechanization and distance; an airborne deus ex machina metastasizing information high above.

Airpower is inextricable from imperial logic; the development of military aviation after World War I is inseparable from surveillance and terror against colonies. A flailing US empire’s assertion of its muscle through “ruling the skies” over Iran is the newest articulation. Migration regimes also connect airborne policing and warfare. Libya surveillance is one example. Another is surging deportation flights (often involving torturous conditions and rendition to hidden camps). These are accompanied by far-right propaganda videos espousing airborne “remigration,” retooling consumerist promises of cheap air travel as instruments of race war. These shows of force themselves suck in resources, from the data center usage involved to aviation fuel.

Seabird is a small counterweight, implicitly posing alternative theories of airpower. Monitoring and rescue infrastructure showcases rapid civil evolution to extreme circumstances. But the entry barrier to airborne operations is even higher than at sea. Regulatory frameworks are tight, operations complex and expensive, and the skill sets and technologies involved are mostly the preserve of military and police forces.

Civilians have limited access to surveillance tech. Sea-Watch trains volunteers to spot potential distress cases with binoculars while flying as slow as the airframe will allow. These processes are developed through trial and error. They are transmitted to volunteers that live on the island for weeks at a time in a shared house, receiving training, orange jumpsuits, and advice to wear a diaper and take motion-sickness pills on one’s first flight. There are high risks of trauma and burnout, perhaps even more so than at sea where crews can at least often directly intervene.

As social, ecological, and technological ruptures deepen, this is one of many environments where emergency response skills are developed alongside political ideas required to apply them.

There’s one more example of the implications of counter-airpower. Last August, I met a Sudanese man who, after fleeing war, was intercepted by Libyan militias at sea. Eventually he was resettled. Rather than moving on, he became involved in advocating for those still suffering and had just returned from flying in Seabird. In the skies, he had reclaimed agency and the ability to assist others.

Our conversation took place in Mérida, Spain, at the end of a scorching summer. Spain was beginning, haltingly, to chart a different path than betting only on higher walls. Madrid recently embarked on migrant regularization, labor law enforcement, a national climate adaptation pact, tech regulation, and standing up against human rights abuses and foreign wars. This is not altruism but self-interest, a pragmatic approach to dangerous times.

The stories that disaster nationalists and fascists tell are simple. It is harder to explain how the mosaic pieces of globalized exploitation fit together. But from the air, you don’t need to: you can look out the window and see storms, pollution, militias, and forced displacement; threads stitching together a tapestry of destruction across the Middle Sea.

After a while, something altogether different emerges. Through distance, the Earth reveals itself unencumbered by transient, shifting borders. We open a window to photograph a rescue vessel below and air rushes in from a bright sea and sky. It becomes easy to imagine different realities.

Back on the ground, tactical coordinator Neeske Beckmann sinks onto a wooden bench among her crew on a rooftop overlooking Lampedusa’s picturesque harbor. After a long flight, she speaks of tiredness and resignation after years of watching nightmares unfold. But just a moment later, she looks at the sky and her shoulders straighten.

“I don’t want to live in a world like this,” she says, more firmly.

“And I refuse to accept it.”

title: Mexican man killed by truck while fleeing ICE in Florida is identified - USA Today
description:
A Mexican national visiting the United States has been identified as the man who died while fleeing from federal immigration officials along a Florida roadway.
He was the third person to die during immigration enforcement operations in a week's span.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers fatally shot a Mexican man July 7 in Texas, and a Colombian man in Maine on July 13.
Mexican officials and a Florida advocacy group confirmed to USA TODAY the person who died was Coronilla Durán.
The same morning, Coronilla Durán became the third person to die during immigration enforcement actions when ICE encountered him at the Florida gas station.
text:
A Mexican national visiting the United States has been identified as the man who died while fleeing from federal immigration officials along a Florida roadway.

On the morning of July 14, Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, 28, was killed after he and three others in a vehicle fled on foot during an encounter with federal immigration officers in a gas station parking lot near St. Augustine.

He was the third person to die during immigration enforcement operations in a week's span. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers fatally shot a Mexican man July 7 in Texas, and a Colombian man in Maine on July 13.

During the July 14 chase, Florida Highway Patrol said a man ran across State Road 16 into the path of an oncoming tractor-trailer and had fatal injuries. State officials didn't disclose Coronilla Durán’s identity. Madison Kessler, an FHP spokesperson, said the agency is investigating the traffic fatality and referred additional questions to the Department of Homeland Security and ICE.

A DHS spokesperson said agency law enforcement officers conducted an operation resulting in a Mexican national dying. Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of ICE, is investigating the death.

Mexican officials and a Florida advocacy group confirmed to USA TODAY the person who died was Coronilla Durán.

He is originally from San Luis de la Paz, a municipality in the central Mexican state of Guanajuato. In emailed responses to USA TODAY, Susana Guerra Vallejo, Guanajuato’s undersecretary for human rights, said the man's wife told Mexican officials he had a visa and had spent a few days in the United States.

The U.S. State Department said it doesn't comment on specific visa cases due to record confidentiality. U.S. Customs and Border Protection, which is part of DHS, didn't respond to an email request for comment. The Mexican Foreign Affairs Ministry didn't respond to email requests for comment.

Isaret Jeffers, founder of the Florida-based farmworkers advocacy organization Colectivo Arbol, told the Associated Press that Coronilla Durán had traveled to visit friends and family in Atlanta and was going to the beach in Florida.

In a phone interview, Jeffers said Coronilla Durán was set to return July 18 to Mexico, where he and his wife live with their two children, ages 7 months and 7 years old. He owns a small restaurant, Jeffers said.

Jeffers said many Latino immigrant families have fear of stepping out of their homes because of immigration enforcement.

"They have fear of leaving and not returning to their children," she said in Spanish.

Adriana Rivera, a spokesperson for the Florida Immigrant Coalition, an advocacy group, said Coronilla Duran's death wasn't an isolated incident as ICE pursues aggressive enforcement. She pointed to the killings of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, in Houston, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 25, in Biddeford, Maine. Both men were shot by ICE officers during traffic stops.

"When federal agents descend on communities and initiate encounters that spark panic and fear, people run," she said in a statement. "They run because they are afraid. They run because they know that an encounter with ICE can mean kidnapping, inhumane detention, family separation, deportation, or death. In the United States, in 2026, whether someone runs or complies with ICE, death is a very real possible outcome.”

Guerra Vallejo, the Guanajuato official, said Coronilla Durán's body hasn’t been repatriated.

On July 14, ICE reportedly halted traffic stops after Salgado Araujo and Durán Guerrero's deaths. Both killings triggered protests, even as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has promised a quieter agency after controversial operations that resulted in the fatal shootings of American citizens by immigration officers in Minneapolis.

A day later, President Donald Trump announced he had reversed the decision. The same morning, Coronilla Durán became the third person to die during immigration enforcement actions when ICE encountered him at the Florida gas station.

On July 15, more than a hundred people protested his death along the Florida roadway where he was killed.
